explanation: No single trigger. It fires on a mix: repeated variable terms in algebra word problems ('*k', '*g', '*s'), number digits, later word-pieces of surnames, URL/code pieces ('.net', 'path', '.onCreate'), and ordinary function words or verbs in prose. The tokens share no common property.

Fires on verbs of deciding or checking (decide, determine, see, know, check, mark) when they introduce an embedded 'whether/if' question, as in 'to decide whether', 'how can I determine', 'to see if'. It also fires on nearby words that set up such a question ('what I want to know is', 'the difference', 'returns'). It is weak or silent when there is no embedded-question frame.

Fires on the first sub-word piece of an identifier or acronym in code or technical text, i.e. a word-piece just after '.', '_', '-' or a space that starts a CamelCase or abbreviated name: 'NSS'ecureCoding, '.w'mode, '_c'bc, 'V'pnSites, 'F'Sharp. It is strongest in source code and include paths, weaker on acronyms in prose (eNOS, SDF), and near zero on normal words.

A mixture. It fires on electronics/semiconductor terms (PMOS, IGBTs, wire bonding, photodiode, potential well), on the indented closing-tag token ' </' in XML/HTML, and on 'links' in the Wikipedia 'External links' heading. It also gives weaker hits on acronyms and on biochemical name endings such as '-in'.

Mainly fires on line-break and brace/paren tokens that end a block in Go source ('}

', ')

' after imports, '

' after a package line, '"

'). It also fires on characters inside non-Latin scripts (Devanagari, Arabic, Greek, Chinese, Cyrillic). Weak scattered hits elsewhere.

Fires on a middle word-piece of a long, rare word or proper name split into several tokens, such as tel'om'erase, gyr(us), Clauser, frank'fur'ters, ole'stra', Yangt'ze', and also on code identifier pieces (\displaystyle, .create, EditorGUI). The strongest case is the inside of scientific terms. Common whole words do not trigger it.

Hard to read. The one clear peak is 'Plus' in 'Eleven Plus'. The other examples, all at about 45-53%, are an unrelated mix: code tokens, idiom endings ('No wonder', 'Sehr gut'), word-pieces in chemical or Turkish words, and prepositions. No shared feature is visible.

Fires on words inside software license and legal boilerplate headers ('compliance with the License', 'obtain a copy', 'is distributed on an AS IS', 'For the full copyright and license information, please') and in similar terms-of-use text ('By using this site you agree to'). It is weak outside such boilerplate.

No clear common feature. It fires on attribute-value openers in HTML/Vue templates (':class="', 'ng-model="', 'checkbox'), 'do' after Elixir function heads, the word 'performance' in tech discussions, and assorted word-pieces and punctuation in code and technical prose.

A mixture. It fires on the 'over' in 'all over' (the world / the place / the country), on '.io' in Java 'import java.io' lines, on markdown/escape syntax (```, table dashes, '\0'), and on characters or word-pieces in non-English text (Romanian, Vietnamese, Chinese/Japanese).

Fires on tokens inside open-source license and copyright header comments: 'See the NOTICE file', 'version 2 only, as published by', 'whose names', 'distributed with', 'for license details', 'license that can be found'. It also fires on similar boilerplate comments in code templates ('Setting ComVisible to false', 'This enables us'). Weak outside header boilerplate.

Fires on tokens that end a clause or open a structure where more text follows: commas before a 'which/depending/however' continuation, '[
', '{
', '(
' that open JSON/arrays, and clause-final words ('at the moment', 'to be exact', 'full stop', 'in addition'). It is also strong on a Chinese adverb. The examples are only loosely unified.

Fires on the token right after an operator or preposition that sets up a value or object: variables after '+', '-', '=' in algebra word problems ('Let h =', '+ w', '- x'), and objects or prepositions in prose ('ate it', 'sending you', 'multiple of', 'goals in'). It also has scattered hits on numbers and word-pieces. The pattern is weakly coherent.

Fires on a capitalized class, API or proper-name token that is the second part of a qualified name, after '.', ':' or a space in code or institutional names: AttributeSet, .onCreate, .Toast, HttpServletRequest, AssemblyCompany, GeneratedValue, localhost in URLs, National End'owment', House 'Judiciary'. Mostly framework or Android/.NET type names.
